About me

Grey-haired software programmer, geek, engineer, and builder of things that probably need another revision.

This is my corner of the internet. It has my CV on it, because that is useful, but mostly it has stuff on it that I think is cool. Because it is cool.

The short version of the story: a BBC Micro, then mechatronics, then motorsport electronics, then Formula One, then thirteen years building a software company and selling it, then an MSc in AI, and now robots. Throughout: a workshop, and a persistent inability to leave things alone.

The through-line

How hard can it be? Then finding out properly.

Every job on this page is a different industry, and they are all the same job. Something has to work in the real world, nobody is completely sure whether it does, and someone has to go and find out. Engine test rigs, payment platforms, robot policies: same question every time. How do we know this is really working?

1984-ish

A BBC Micro, and a book of listings

My dad bought a BBC B. I learned that computers were not sealed appliances: you could type a listing out of a book, make a mistake, find the mistake, fix it, and then a machine did something because you had told it to.

That is still the whole thing, really. Everything after this is the same loop with more expensive equipment.

School

A hovercraft, and a robot CD player

A hovercraft for GCSE. A robot CD player at A level. Both start as slightly ridiculous ideas and then turn into engineering somewhere around the point you realise the thing has to actually work on the day.

1997

Mechatronics at Leeds

BEng in Mechatronics: the degree for people who cannot decide between mechanical, electronic and software engineering, and would rather not. My final-year project was a robotic chessboard, which won an award and moved the pieces itself.

1997–2003

Motorsport electronics

Pi Research, later Cosworth. Embedded C, engine controllers, sensors, wiring looms, CAN and serial integration, telemetry, fuel simulation, engine-test automation.

Trackside debugging is a particular education. The car is on the grid, the data says one thing, the engine says another, and there is no useful sense in which you can ask for more time.

2003–2006

Formula One

Two years at Jaguar Racing programme-managing the cross-functional design, manufacture and build of race-ready cars, then R&D at Red Bull Racing on sensors, actuators, software, hardware and automated systems.

F1 is the most concentrated example I have seen of the thing I keep coming back to: an enormous number of specialists, one physical object, and a deadline that does not move.

2006–2019

Co-founding Aeriandi

Thirteen years co-founding and building a secure B2B SaaS company, as CTO and chief architect, and hands-on the whole way. We ended up with 40 staff, £8M ARR, and a patented PCI voice-payment platform carrying more than half of UK utilities' phone payments.

I learned what a company actually is here, which is mostly: hiring, trust, compliance, and being the person who is awake when the platform is not.

2019–2024

Merger, acquisition, and the other side of it

Aeriandi merged with Voxygen to become Speik, which was then acquired by Dubber, where I ran technical strategy, platform reliability and compliance for EMEA. Around 300 production services across AWS, Azure and on-prem.

Also, in parallel and slightly insanely, I was principal contractor on a self-built family home. The one with the curved walls.

2025–2026

Going back to school on purpose

An AI residency at the ML Institute, then an MSc in Artificial Intelligence at Leeds, finished with Distinction. Nine taught modules and a dissertation on robot learning: MuJoCo simulation, teleoperation through a VR headset, PyTorch policies, and then the awkward business of testing them on hardware that has friction in it.

Now

Robots, and a workshop

Staff engineer at NeoIntralogistics, building warehouse systems that coordinate autonomous mobile robots and Universal Robots arms. Which is, pleasingly, the BBC Micro problem again: make the machine do the thing, then work out whether it really did it.

The rest of the time I am in the workshop, and that is what most of this site is about.

What I care about

Three things I keep coming back to

Real evidence

I want to know whether a system is actually better, not whether the graph looks nicer.

Open teams

Trust, challenge, humour and people playing their position on the pitch.

Physical consequences

Software is more interesting when it moves hardware, handles real users or has to survive reality.

Contact

Say hello.

Oxford, UK. Happy to talk about robots, reliability, steel, or why your simulator is lying to you.
